articles.title: Christopher Nemeth: a Tokyo castle of post-punk design
articles.content: Christopher Nemeth: a Tokyo castle of post-punk design on x (opens in a new window) Christopher Nemeth: a Tokyo castle of post-punk design on facebook (opens in a new window) Christopher Nemeth: a Tokyo castle of post-punk design on linkedin (opens in a new window) Christopher Nemeth: a Tokyo castle of post-punk design on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Christopher Nemeth: a Tokyo castle of post-punk design on x (opens in a new window) Christopher Nemeth: a Tokyo castle of post-punk design on facebook (opens in a new window) Christopher Nemeth: a Tokyo castle of post-punk design on linkedin (opens in a new window) Christopher Nemeth: a Tokyo castle of post-punk design on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Words and photography by Mark C O’Flaherty Published May 21 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Omotesandō in Tokyo is a neighbourhood for fashion pilgrimage – its main stretch has been home to flagship stores for Comme des Garçons, Issey Miyake and Yohji Yamamoto since the 1980s. But those once rarefied brands are now global entities. In a side street nearby is the only Christopher Nemeth shop in the world, selling the work of one of the most innovative designers of the London post-punk scene. It’s a diamond in the rough – independent, atmospheric, edgy, often chaotic. Every surface is covered in the well-worn, dark, richly geometric and witchy wallpaper created by Nemeth in 1989. There are garments made with a fabric created to feel like canvas used for oil paintings, and boards full of plaid and dogtooth badges, ready to customise anything to which you can pin them. The shop’s exterior © Mark C O’Flaherty While you can buy selected Nemeth garments in branches of Dover Street Market , this is where obsessives come for seasonal one-off and limited pieces, including bolero-length jackets made from Nemeth’s No 1 pattern, often bearing his distinctive Isle Rope print (from ¥93,000, about £430), and variations on his curved-leg jeans with XL turn-ups and distressed knee details (from about £130). Nemeth was initially categorised as a menswear designer, but his irreverent approach made for genderless tailoring. The clothes have been sold on the Tokyo site since the mid-1980s, when his wife, Keiko, ran a shop there; in 1994, it became an eponymous store dedicated solely to his work. He died aged 51 in 2010. Now Keiko and their daughters, Lui and Riyo (both formally trained artists), run the business. “I remember when I was at primary school and dad just had a small workroom, doing it all himself,” says Riyo, who is often behind the counter. “My mum worked out production and she still has everything made here in Japan.” Christopher Nemeth No 1 jacket, about £465, made using deadstock fabrics from the UK © Mark C O’Flaherty Badges featuring Nemeth prints, from simple plastic buttons, about £1.40, to fabric-covered pieces, about £3.70 © Mark C O’Flaherty There was a resurgence in interest in Nemeth’s clothing after his death. The family kept the label in production (Lui manages the wholesale for Dover Street Market), and in 2015 Kim Jones worked with them to incorporate prints from the archive into his AW15 collection for Louis Vuitton. Jones had been a Nemeth fan for decades, obsessed with the legacy of the House of Beauty and Culture, the rarely open store that existed in Dalston from 1986 to 1989. Hobac (as it’s commonly referred to) was a design and arts collective founded by shoe designer John Moore that included Nemeth, furniture makers Frick and Frack, knitwear designer Richard Torry, artist Dave Baby and jewellery maker Judy Blame. The group honed a look that lives on in Omotesandō today. Christopher Nemeth wool overcoat in Isle Rope print, about £765 © Mark C O’Flaherty Christopher Nemeth Isle Rope print bag, about £205, handmade in Turkey © Mark C O’Flaherty When Nemeth left for Japan in 1986, just as the London shop was gaining traction, he’d acquired cult status for his deconstructed, upcycled clothes. Core Hobac members Blame and fashion photographer Mark Lebon (who had put Nemeth’s work in key editorial spreads) made regular trips to Tokyo to continue collaborating. What they created is the soul of the shop today. Nemeth’s art hangs on the wall; included on the rack are No 1 and 19B jackets, from about £558 and about £385, and 336BW coats, from about £450 © Mark C O’Flaherty Most of what made London so radical in the mid-1980s is gone. As are Blame and Nemeth. But the Tokyo store and its product remain in the present tense. Keiko’s daughters say their mother sees the store as “her castle”. From the round linen holdalls emblazoned with Nemeth’s rope print (from about £140) to the artworks on the wall that aren’t for sale, it merges counterculture art and retail in a way reminiscent of Keith Haring’s extinct Pop Shop and McLaren and Westwood’s World’s End. Nemeth’s early samples are sought after at auction, and Hobac nostalgia shows no sign of fading. It’s thrilling and poignant to be able to walk into the Tokyo store and buy authentic clothes, 40 years after their designer first moved here. 4 Chome-13-5 Jingūmae, Shibuya, Tokyo 150-0001; christophernemeth.co Reuse this content (opens in new window) Comments Jump to comments section Follow the topics in this article Menswear Shopping in Tokyo Style Fashion Cult Shop Comments

articles.title: Stunt performer Ayesha Hussain’s guide to Ouarzazate – ‘the Hollywood of Africa’
articles.content: Stunt performer Ayesha Hussain’s guide to Ouarzazate – ‘the Hollywood of Africa’ on x (opens in a new window) Stunt performer Ayesha Hussain’s guide to Ouarzazate – ‘the Hollywood of Africa’ on facebook (opens in a new window) Stunt performer Ayesha Hussain’s guide to Ouarzazate – ‘the Hollywood of Africa’ on linkedin (opens in a new window) Stunt performer Ayesha Hussain’s guide to Ouarzazate – ‘the Hollywood of Africa’ on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Stunt performer Ayesha Hussain’s guide to Ouarzazate – ‘the Hollywood of Africa’ on x (opens in a new window) Stunt performer Ayesha Hussain’s guide to Ouarzazate – ‘the Hollywood of Africa’ on facebook (opens in a new window) Stunt performer Ayesha Hussain’s guide to Ouarzazate – ‘the Hollywood of Africa’ on linkedin (opens in a new window) Stunt performer Ayesha Hussain’s guide to Ouarzazate – ‘the Hollywood of Africa’ on whatsapp (opens in a new window) As told to Rosanna Dodds . Photography by Ismail Zaidy Published May 21 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. I stumbled upon Ouarzazate, a city south of Morocco’s High Atlas mountains, by accident. It was 2019 and I was on my way from Marrakech to the Merzouga desert. We stopped off for a night at La Palmeraie, the most stunning eco-lodge. There were rescued animals – peacocks and goats – walking about, and loads of hammocks to lie in. It was so off-the-beaten-track. I was like… “Wow.” The village of Aït Benhaddou © Ismail Zaidy Morocco is the only place my mother, sisters and I went on holiday – it was a single trip to Marrakech in 2012 that’s been immortalised in our brains forever. That was before I’d started riding: it was the first place I’d ever seen people on horses. We came across a horse show and we were absolutely mesmerised. My mum died in 2022, and Morocco has been a special place for my sisters and I ever since; it’s sort of emblematic of her. Hussain with a horse © Ismail Zaidy Hussain rides through Kasbah Aït Benhaddou © Ismail Zaidy Ouarzazate is more of a rustic adventure playground than a have-a-nice-drink-at-a-bar kind of place. Because of how rural it is, I didn’t imagine there would be any circumstances in which I’d end up back there, but four years after my first trip to the city, my stunt co-ordinator called me up to say that I’d be living there for a month to film Gladiator II . The city’s vastness and proximity to the desert means that the film scene is crazy. There’s a bunch of studios near there; people call it “the Hollywood of Africa”. I got into stunt work – and through that, horse-riding – when I got scouted for Playboy in my first year of university (I was hosting parties in France and Switzerland as opposed to getting my bits out). That put me on the path to being a cabaret performer, through which I met a (now ex-) boyfriend. He was a circus strongman. He introduced me to knife-throwing, which became my predominant stage skill. Hussain rides a horse at Kasbah Aït Benhaddou © Ismail Zaidy The rooftop terrace at Taman’Art Space © Haytham Laalilis (aka The Hatman) Around that time I did a heritage deep dive with my mum. I knew we were Indian and Arab, but from where exactly, I didn’t know. She revealed that we are descendants of the Rajputs, the most prolific warrior clan in India. They trained their women to use swords – and they were also skilled in horsemanship. I started training in sword combat to honour that heritage, and was eventually convinced to train for the stunt register. I’m still training: you need to qualify to a really high standard in six different sports. One of mine is horse-riding. Now the majority of my work tends to be fighting and horses. For Deadpool it was mostly superhero fights. Doctor Who was a lot of wire work and flying around, as you do. And for Gladiator II I was part of a team of six female stunt archers. We basically spent three weeks on the top of a turret in 36°C heat, repetitively doing formation firing. Hussain in Aït Benhaddou © Ismail Zaidy BARS, CAFÉS & RESTAURANTS Café Restaurant Moussa @cafe_restaurant_moussa Le Jardin des Arômes @jardindesaromesozz SHOPPING Ouarzazate Souk Avenue Moulay Ettahar Ben Abdulkarim, 45000 Ouarzazate THINGS TO DO Taman’Art Space @tamanart_space WHERE TO STAY La Palmeraie Ecolodge Ouarzazate ecolodge-palmeraie-ouarzazate.com Ranch Baikan @horseback_aitbenhaddou I wanted to find somewhere I could ride while filming in Ouarzazate – somewhere that treated its horses well, which can be difficult to find in other countries. Someone recommended Ranch Baikan in Aït Benhaddou, a village a half-hour drive from the city centre. It’s where they filmed Lawrence of Arabia , The Mummy and parts of the original Gladiator . Ranch Baikan isn’t bougie – it’s actually quite simple – but it’s beautifully laid out, with a little indoor swimming pool and the most amazing horses. It’s also small; it’s only got six or seven rooms. But when you walk out onto your balcony you’re surrounded by open plains. The stars are the brightest you’ve ever seen. The area is peppered with loads of lovely restaurants. You can get some more European-style cuisine, but the majority of it is warm, hearty Arabian flavours – the kind of images that might come to mind when you think about Morocco. Lots of tagines. Amazingly cooked meat. Le Jardin des Arômes does a stunning lamb tagine with dates: Pedro Pascal went there quite a lot when we were filming Gladiator II . More recently I’ve been to Café Restaurant Moussa; they do an unbelievable virgin Mojito. Hussain rides through Aït Benhaddou © Ismail Zaidy Bungalows at La Palmeraie Ecolodge © La Palmeraie Ecolodge The souks in general are also amazing. Head in to town to the old market, which is great for things like antiques and cool furniture. The main souk is covered wall to wall in beautiful textiles and jewellery. Aït Benhaddou’s old city complex is similarly full of little shops – intricate lamps and unbelievable tea sets. The furniture and kitchenware is elite. The thing I find nicest about Ouarzazate is that I can walk around at night and feel safe. When I think about being in Marrakech on my own, I can find it heady and a little pushy. In Ouarzazate it feels like an entire community has been woven through it. I find that quite magical. Last time I was there I visited Taman’Art Space, a traditional desert blues space in Aït Benhaddou – the local talent was global-stage level. I’ve ended up getting to know Brahim, who runs Ranch Baikan, quite well. After I finished filming Gladiator II , I stayed an extra week. When my mum died, I knew I wanted to go to Morocco and ride horses in her honour. Coincidentally, the film wrapped the week before her birthday. The ranch had just had a new horse arrive, and all the women from the village cooked an amazing feast to welcome it. It was also a heavenly birthday celebration for my mum. The whole thing was crazy. Anyone who experiences Ouarzazate will be mesmerised in the same way that I am. My heritage, my bond with the horses, my utter love for them – and then my mum – all of those things keep me tethered to the land.
